posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-value ICP prospects (VP Ops, COO, CEO) engaging on a compliance-driven AI ban — validate the auditability problem and add the 'explainability as the real unlock' insight without pitching
posts.draft_comment: The ban makes complete sense honestly. 'GPT said so' isn't an audit trail, it's a liability. The thing regulators and analysts both need isn't just the right number — it's a clear line back to where it came from and why. Wonder how many teams are quietly in the same position but haven't hit that regulator moment yet.

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO frustrated with Power BI adoption failure — validate the trust gap insight, add the 'numbers without provenance' layer, leave Milo out entirely
posts.draft_comment: The trust problem is underrated. People don't distrust the dashboard, they distrust not being able to explain where the number came from when someone challenges it in the room. Excel feels safer because everyone can see the working. How do you build that same auditability into something that isn't a spreadsheet?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging with a post that validates dashboard overload — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add the 'why nobody looks' layer, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs is basically a confidence problem dressed up as a reporting problem — if you're not sure what matters, you measure everything and hope nobody notices. The jump from 10% to 85% usage tells the real story though. People don't avoid dashboards because they're lazy, they avoid them because they've learned the dashboard won't actually help them make a call. What made those 5 the right 5?

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: Innovation Director at NorthStar Retail is engaging on a post about BI chaos — validate the 'who owns truth' pain with a sharper reframe, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: Three definitions of revenue is almost a rite of passage at this point. The tool was never really the problem — it's that self-service BI assumed shared understanding of the data before anyone had actually built it. You can democratise access all you want, but if finance and marketing are starting from different places, more dashboards just means more confident arguments about the wrong number. Who actually gets to call the final answer in your org?

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO framing hallucinations as security risk with CEO of 90-person data company engaging — validate the reframe, add the trust layer insight, no pitch needed
posts.draft_comment: The framing shift here is important — hallucinations aren't just wrong, they're unverifiable by most people reading the output. A CFO doesn't know to distrust a number that looks right. That's the actual risk: not that the AI is wrong, but that there's no natural moment where anyone thinks to check. How do you build scrutiny into a workflow when the whole appeal of the tool is that you stopped having to scrutinise?

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: ICP prospect (COO at Sterling Consulting) engaging with a post about BI tools failing non-technical users — validate the specific pain of the £200k ghost tool, add the insight that adoption is a design problem not a training problem
posts.draft_comment: That £200k platform sitting unused is almost never a data quality problem or even a complexity problem — it's a design problem. Most BI tools were built to impress the person buying them, not the person who needs to answer a question at 9am on a Monday. The vendor demo always shows a data analyst. The real user is someone who just needs to know if the numbers are good or bad. How many of your clients have a tool like that quietly gathering dust right now?

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director calling out a data governance/culture problem that's actually a definition problem — validate the real diagnosis and add the layer most people miss
posts.draft_comment: Three teams, same dataset, three answers — that's not a culture problem, that's a definitions problem dressed up as one. Nobody agreed on what 'revenue' means before they built the dashboard. Culture gets blamed a lot for things that were actually just skipped conversations at the start of a project. Did the CFO ask who owns the definition, or just who owns the dashboard?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing the 'nobody knows what to ask' problem — validate the adoption failure pattern and add the insight that the real gap is context, not capability
posts.draft_comment: That 12% number is painfully familiar. The issue isn't that people don't want to use it — it's that a blank prompt box is terrifying if you don't already know what you're looking for. Shadow AI filling the gap makes total sense, it's lower stakes to just ask ChatGPT on your phone than to look clueless in a corporate tool. Curious whether you think the fix is training, or whether the tool itself needs to do more of the work of surfacing the right questions?
